Q116236478.summary: On this tiny plaque, barely four centimetres high, Christ hangs on the cross with arms outstretched along the beam, his head inclined and nimbed, wearing a long knotted loincloth, his feet resting on a small mound. Two haloed mourners — presumably the Virgin and St John — stand beneath the arms of the cross, each raising a hand to the cheek in grief, while two angels lean over the crossbeam above. Traces of gilding remain on the haloes.
facts: The Met dates the plaque to about 1000 (995–1005) and classes it as Ottonian; it measures only 4.1 × 2.8 cm.
It was given to the Metropolitan Museum by J. Pierpont Morgan in 1917.
The gesture of hand to cheek is a long-established sign of mourning in Crucifixion imagery of this period.

links.label: The Met: Ivory Plaque with the Crucifixion

Q116236478.notes: The Met's date of c. 1000 sits on the boundary of the early period. Which mourner is the Virgin and which John cannot be confirmed from the small photograph.

yuag:93256.summary: On the face of this gold coin Christ appears as a bust with long hair and a full beard, a cross behind his head, raising his right hand in blessing and holding the book of the Gospels. The legend names him 'Jesus Christ, King of those who reign'. On the reverse the emperor stands in consular robes holding a cross on steps, with the title 'servant of Christ', so the coin itself declares who is the true sovereign.
facts: Justinian II was the first Byzantine emperor to put the image of Christ on coins issued in his name; this long-haired type belongs to his first reign (685–695).
Yale records the legends as IHSUS XRISTUS REX REGNANTIUM on the obverse and IUSTINIANUS SERVUS XRISTI on the reverse, with the mint mark COMOB.
The coin weighs 4.43 g and was struck at Constantinople; it came to Yale from Professor Alfred R. Bellinger.
yuag:93256.notes: A different specimen of the same type as other Justinian II solidi in the collection, not a duplicate object.
